lessons.title: Jacobians and local linearization
lessons.subtitle: Retain first-order change near equilibrium

body.title: Find equilibria first
body.text: For $\mathbf x'=\mathbf f(\mathbf x)$, solve $\mathbf f(\mathbf x_*)=0$ before applying equilibrium tests. An arbitrary point is not an equilibrium.

body.title: The first-order matrix
body.text: In displacement coordinates, $\mathbf u'=J\mathbf u+\mathbf r(\mathbf u)$, with remainder small relative to displacement. $J$ is the derivative matrix at equilibrium.

body.title: Which conclusions are reliable?
body.text: Strictly negative real parts give local asymptotic stability; a positive real part gives instability. Zero real parts can make linearization inconclusive, especially near a center.

derivation.text: Translate equilibrium to the origin.
Use the multivariable first-order expansion.
derivation.latex: \mathbf f(\mathbf x_*+\mathbf u)=J\mathbf u+\mathbf r(\mathbf u)

derivation.text: For hyperbolic cases, sufficiently small higher-order terms do not overturn the linear trend.

workedExamples.title: A locally stable model
steps: Both real parts are strictly negative.
workedExamples.answer: Locally asymptotically stable, without claiming global attraction.

workedExamples.title: Zero roots are inconclusive
steps: The first points inward on both sides and the second outward.

practice.problem: Find the Jacobian of $x'=2x+xy,y'=-y$ at the origin.
solution: Cross terms have no first-order contribution at zero.

practice.problem: Classify the origin for $x^\prime=2x+xy,y^\prime=-y$.
solution: An expanding direction exists.

practice.problem: Do purely imaginary linear roots prove a nonlinear center?
solution: The linear part only rotates; higher-order radial effects may matter.

practice.problem: Does local asymptotic stability mean every distant initial state converges there?
solution: Other equilibria or escaping trajectories may exist.

commonMistakes.claim: Use the Jacobian at any point to classify an equilibrium.
commonMistakes.correction: Verify it is an equilibrium first.

commonMistakes.claim: A linearized center guarantees a nonlinear center.
commonMistakes.correction: Higher-order terms can determine stability with zero real parts.

lessons.concept: The Jacobian gives a nonlinear system's first-order model near equilibrium. Hyperbolic stability types can be classified by that linearization.
lessons.intuition: Magnify the neighborhood and ask whether its first-order change already determines the trend.

formalDefinition.latex: J=D\mathbf f(\mathbf x_*),\quad\mathbf u'=J\mathbf u+o(\lVert\mathbf u\rVert)
conditions: The right-hand side is continuously differentiable near equilibrium. An equilibrium without zero-real-part eigenvalues is hyperbolic. Conclusions are local, not automatically global.

learningCheck.question: If all Jacobian eigenvalues have strictly negative real parts, what follows?
choices: Every nearby solution is a line
Every state globally tends to zero
learningCheck.explanation: This is a local result with hypotheses.

teaching.explain: Linearization magnifies a neighborhood; it does not replace the entire nonlinear system everywhere with a matrix.

steps.title: Near the origin
steps.observation: The two trajectories remain close and approach zero.
steps.instruction: Set initial first component $x_0$ to $0.2$, initial second component $y_0$ to $0.5$, and observation time $t$ to $3$.

steps.title: Farther away, below the threshold
steps.observation: Nonlinear effects are stronger, but the solution still tends to zero.
steps.instruction: Set initial first component $x_0$ to $0.8$, initial second component $y_0$ to $1$, and observation time $t$ to $3$.

steps.title: Beyond the threshold
steps.observation: A finite window or solution endpoint is reported; local stability cannot establish global attraction.
steps.instruction: Set initial first component $x_0$ to $1.5$, initial second component $y_0$ to $0$, and observation time $t$ to $3$.

interactiveVisual.caption: Compare nonlinear and local-linear phase trajectories. The origin attracts only locally; beyond first-component threshold one, trajectories may escape and blow up.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does the near-origin conclusion extend to the other side of the threshold?

lessons.title: Nullclines and predator-prey models
lessons.subtitle: One stationary component need not mean a stationary state

body.title: Define two nullcline families
body.text: In planar system $x'=f,y'=g$, $f=0$ is the horizontal-component nullcline and $g=0$ the vertical-component nullcline.

body.title: An idealized model
body.text: Use $x'=x(1-y),y'=y(x-1)$. Positive states represent two populations coupled by encounter rates; resource limits and other realistic mechanisms are absent.

body.title: What does the picture show?
body.text: In the first quadrant, thresholds at one determine directions. Nullclines are generally not trajectories. A numerically closed curve does not prove periodic solutions for general models.

derivation.text: Set the two components to zero separately.
The other component gives the other family.
Simultaneous zeros give equilibria.

workedExamples.title: Read directions
workedExamples.problem: At state $(2,1/2)$, which way does motion go?

workedExamples.title: A nullcline point need not be equilibrium
steps: Its vertical derivative is one, so motion continues upward.

practice.problem: What are the two non-axis nullclines in the positive quadrant?
solution: The horizontal-component nullcline is horizontal at one; the vertical-component nullcline is vertical at one.

practice.problem: At $(1/2,2)$, does each component increase or decrease?
solution: The horizontal factor and vertical threshold difference are negative.

practice.problem: Where is the positive equilibrium?
solution: Both coordinates are one.

practice.problem: Must an entire nullcline be a solution trajectory?
practice.hint: The other component can move the state off the line.
solution: One vanishing derivative is not enough to stay there.

commonMistakes.claim: One component's zero derivative means equilibrium.
commonMistakes.correction: Every component must vanish simultaneously.

commonMistakes.claim: An ideal predator-prey model directly predicts every real ecosystem.
commonMistakes.correction: Parameters and missing mechanisms limit its scope.

lessons.concept: Nullclines divide phase space into component-increase and decrease regions; their intersections are equilibria.
lessons.intuition: A nullcline can pause one component while the other continues moving.
objectives: Interpret directions in the positive-state region

conditions: Population meaning uses $x,y>0$. The axes are invariant; numerical methods should check for accidental escape from the positive region.

learningCheck.question: How are equilibria related to the two nullcline families?
learningCheck.explanation: Every state component must be stationary together.

teaching.explain: Use nullclines to divide the plane, then read the signs within regions before interpreting trajectories.

steps.title: Positive equilibrium
steps.observation: Both populations stay fixed.
steps.instruction: Set initial population $x_0$ to $1$, initial population $y_0$ to $1$, and observation time $t$ to $5$.

steps.title: Away from equilibrium
steps.observation: Motion crosses regions with different signs.
steps.instruction: Set initial population $x_0$ to $1.5$, initial population $y_0$ to $0.5$, and observation time $t$ to $5$.

steps.title: Another starting state
steps.observation: Nullcline regions explain initial decline and later turning.
steps.instruction: Set initial population $x_0$ to $0.5$, initial population $y_0$ to $1.5$, and observation time $t$ to $5$.

interactiveVisual.caption: The phase plane shows nullclines, a direction field, and an RK4 approximation in the positive region. A finite numerical trajectory is not a proof of periodicity.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does every point on a nullcline remain stationary?

lessons.title: Energy, pendulums, and Lyapunov functions
lessons.subtitle: Find a quantity that cannot increase

body.title: The pendulum state equation
body.text: With dimensionless time, use $\theta'=v,v'=-\sin\theta-cv$. A small-angle linearization cannot replace large-angle motion.

body.title: How does energy evolve?
body.text: Choose $E=v^2/2+1-\cos\theta$ to obtain $E'=-cv^2$. Energy is conserved without damping and nonincreasing with damping.

body.title: Nonincrease does not yet prove convergence
body.text: Zero derivative may occur on a whole set. To prove asymptotic convergence, analyze the invariant motions possible within it. A nonpositive derivative alone is insufficient.

derivation.text: Differentiate along a solution.
Substitute both state equations.
The restoring-force terms cancel.

workedExamples.title: An undamped pendulum
workedExamples.problem: With $c=0$ starting at $(\theta,v)=(0,1)$, find the energy.
steps: Kinetic energy is half the squared speed.

practice.problem: What is the energy at the stationary bottom equilibrium?
practice.hint: Both angle and velocity are zero.
solution: Both terms vanish.

practice.problem: Does nonzero small oscillation eventually stop without damping?
solution: It cannot approach the zero-energy bottom state.

practice.problem: What energy does a stationary pendulum at the top have?
Does a nonpositive Lyapunov derivative automatically prove asymptotic stability?
practice.hint: Its zero-derivative set may support continuing motion.
solution: The undamped oscillator is a counterexample.

commonMistakes.claim: Nonincreasing energy means it strictly decreases immediately everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: At zero velocity, its instantaneous derivative can vanish.

commonMistakes.claim: Small-angle approximation exactly describes full rotations.
commonMistakes.correction: The sine approximation needs sufficiently small angles.

lessons.concept: Energy or a Lyapunov function controls a whole state using one scalar without solving every trajectory.
lessons.intuition: A positive measure of distance from equilibrium that cannot increase restricts how far trajectories can move away.

conditions: Assume $c\ge0$. Energy is positive definite near the bottom equilibrium. Physical angles are modulo $2\pi$; top equilibria and high-energy rotations need separate analysis.

learningCheck.question: How does undamped pendulum energy change?
learningCheck.explanation: Kinetic and potential energy exchange while their sum is conserved.

teaching.explain: Energy compares two-dimensional motion with one quantity. Staying close and eventually stopping still need distinct proofs.

steps.title: No damping
steps.observation: Numerical energy is approximately conserved; theoretical energy is exactly conserved.
steps.instruction: Set initial angle $\theta_0$ to $1.5$, damping coefficient $c$ to $0$, and observation time $t$ to $6$.

steps.title: With damping
steps.observation: Trajectories contract and energy is nonincreasing.
steps.instruction: Set initial angle $\theta_0$ to $1.5$, damping coefficient $c$ to $0.5$, and observation time $t$ to $6$.

steps.title: Small angle
steps.observation: Local motion approximates a linear oscillator.
steps.instruction: Set initial angle $\theta_0$ to $0.2$, damping coefficient $c$ to $0.2$, and observation time $t$ to $6$.

interactiveVisual.caption: Phase angle is not wrapped and initial velocity is zero. Readouts give RK4 state and energy; analytic dissipation establishes the energy trend.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How do energy and phase trajectories change when damping is removed?

lessons.title: Parameters and basic bifurcations
lessons.subtitle: Continuous parameter changes can alter equilibria

body.title: A saddle-node model
body.text: $y'=\mu-y^2$ has no equilibrium for negative parameter, a double equilibrium at zero, and two equilibria for positive parameter, one stable and one unstable.

body.title: A pitchfork model
body.text: $y'=\mu y-y^3$ always has the zero equilibrium. Positive parameters create two stable nonzero equilibria while the origin becomes unstable.

body.title: A parameter is not time
body.text: A bifurcation diagram compares systems with different fixed parameters. Automatically sweeping a slider compares models; it does not solve an equation with time-varying parameters.

derivation.text: Find the equilibrium condition.
Positive parameters give two roots; negative ones no real roots.
Classify using the state derivative.

workedExamples.title: Saddle-node parameter four
steps: The equilibria are plus and minus two.
The state derivative is negative at plus two and positive at minus two.
workedExamples.answer: Plus two is stable; minus two unstable.

workedExamples.title: Pitchfork parameter one
steps: The roots are zero and plus and minus one.
workedExamples.answer: Zero is unstable; plus and minus one are asymptotically stable.

practice.problem: Does $y'=-1-y^2$ have real equilibria?
practice.hint: Set the right-hand side to zero.
solution: It would require a square equal to minus one, which is impossible.

practice.problem: How do the sides of zero behave in $y'=-y^2$?
practice.hint: The right side is negative on both sides.
solution: Positive states approach zero; negative states leave.

practice.problem: How does the pitchfork origin behave for negative parameters?
practice.hint: The linear derivative equals the parameter.
solution: A negative derivative gives local asymptotic stability.

practice.problem: Can a parameter-sweep animation be treated as a nonautonomous solution?
practice.hint: Every frame uses another fixed-parameter system.
solution: Actual time dependence of a parameter must be put into the equation and solved.

commonMistakes.claim: A repeated equilibrium determines stability by itself.
commonMistakes.correction: A zero linear term needs further analysis.

commonMistakes.claim: A bifurcation diagram is one initial-value trajectory over time.
commonMistakes.correction: It records equilibrium structures at fixed parameter values.

lessons.concept: A bifurcation is a change in equilibrium count or stability structure as a parameter crosses a critical value.
lessons.intuition: It reorganizes a family of nearby motions, rather than merely changing one curve's appearance.
objectives: Analyze saddle-node and pitchfork normal forms
Distinguish fixed-parameter comparisons from time-dependent parameters

conditions: The parameter is fixed and real. The positive root has negative derivative, the negative root positive derivative. At zero, use signs rather than only linear derivatives.

learningCheck.question: Which change concerns bifurcation?
choices: A parameter changes equilibrium or stability structure
learningCheck.explanation: Structural change is the key.

teaching.explain: Fix a parameter and study that system before comparing parameter values. This separates bifurcation from time evolution.

steps.title: Negative parameter
steps.observation: No real equilibrium; state decreases.
steps.instruction: Set fixed parameter $\mu$ to $-1$, initial value $y_0$ to $0$, and observation time $t$ to $1$.

steps.title: Threshold
steps.observation: Zero initial data stay at the double equilibrium.
steps.instruction: Set fixed parameter $\mu$ to $0$, initial value $y_0$ to $0$, and observation time $t$ to $1$.

steps.title: Positive parameter
steps.observation: Zero initial data approach stable equilibrium one.
steps.instruction: Set fixed parameter $\mu$ to $1$, initial value $y_0$ to $0$, and observation time $t$ to $2$.

interactiveVisual.caption: Horizontal is time, showing a fixed-parameter solution and equilibrium lines when present. Automatic sweeping compares different systems, rather than solving time-varying parameter dynamics.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How many equilibria appear when the fixed parameter changes from negative to positive?

lessons.title: Power-series solutions at ordinary points
lessons.subtitle: Turn a function into a coefficient sequence

body.title: What is an ordinary point?
body.text: If the standard second-order coefficients are analytic near the expansion point, it is ordinary and solutions have local Taylor series.

body.title: How do you align powers?
body.text: After differentiation, shift indices to express every sum in the same power. Check lowest terms separately rather than dropping them.

body.title: Truncations are not exact solutions
body.text: A finite partial sum usually satisfies the equation only approximately. Coefficient analyticity supplies a lower bound for convergence radius; a particular solution may extend farther.

derivation.text: Substitute $y''+y=0$.
Every coefficient must vanish.
Initial data fix the even and odd chains.

practice.problem: In the recurrence for $y''+y=0$, how are $a_4$ and $a_2$ related?
practice.hint: Set the recurrence index to two.

practice.problem: Which familiar solution matches $a_0=0,a_1=1$?
solution: The result is $t-t^3/6+\cdots$.

practice.problem: Does a finite series truncation usually solve the equation exactly?
solution: Exactness occurs only in special terminating cases.

practice.problem: Why does the constant term of $y''=ty$ give $a_2=0$?
practice.hint: Multiplication by time leaves no constant on the right.
solution: The left constant is $2a_2$.

commonMistakes.claim: Index shifts need no check of starting terms.
commonMistakes.correction: The lowest summation terms may need separate treatment.

commonMistakes.claim: Agreement after plotting more terms proves convergence.
commonMistakes.correction: Convergence requires analytic theory or an independent estimate.

lessons.concept: Near an ordinary point, substitute a power series and compare like powers to derive a recurrence.
lessons.intuition: Initial data fix the first coefficients; the equation supplies later ones in order.
objectives: Distinguish an infinite-series solution from a finite approximation

conditions: In standard homogeneous $y^{\prime\prime}+P(t)y^\prime+Q(t)y=0$, coefficients $P,Q$ are analytic near the expansion point. Continuity alone does not guarantee analytic solutions.
Differentiate termwise within the convergence disk. We expand at ordinary point zero; shift the variable for another center.

learningCheck.question: Which initial coefficients determine a second-order ordinary-point solution?
learningCheck.explanation: They represent initial value and initial derivative.

teaching.explain: Series methods complete the solution through coefficients rather than through successive function values.

steps.title: Degree-two truncation
steps.observation: Only constant and quadratic terms remain.
steps.instruction: Set truncation degree $n$ to $2$ and observation time $t$ to $1$.

steps.title: Degree-six truncation
steps.observation: Error is smaller in the same window.
steps.instruction: Set truncation degree $n$ to $6$ and observation time $t$ to $2$.

steps.title: Degree-twelve truncation
steps.observation: More terms improve the fit, but it remains a finite approximation.
steps.instruction: Set truncation degree $n$ to $12$ and observation time $t$ to $3$.

interactiveVisual.caption: Gold retains terms up to the chosen degree; blue is exact cosine. Compare function error and equation residual.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How do function error and equation residual change with truncation degree?

lessons.title: Regular singular points and indicial equations
lessons.subtitle: Let a solution begin with a fractional power

body.title: Check the singularity type first
body.text: For $y''+P(t)y'+Q(t)y=0$, if $tP(t)$ and $t^2Q(t)$ are analytic at zero, zero is a regular singular point.

body.title: Trial form
body.text: On positive time, use $y=t^r\sum a_nt^n$ with $a_0\ne0$. The lowest-power term yields the indicial equation.

body.title: What do the roots determine?
body.text: Indicial roots give possible starting powers. A noninteger root difference usually gives two Frobenius solutions; integer differences and repeated roots need further analysis and may introduce logarithms.

derivation.text: Write the lowest-order terms.
derivation.latex: y\sim a_0t^r,\quad y'\sim ra_0t^{r-1},\quad y''\sim r(r-1)a_0t^{r-2}

derivation.text: Retain the coefficient of the smallest power.
A nonzero leading coefficient forces the bracket to vanish.

workedExamples.title: Distinct indicial roots
workedExamples.answer: $r=1,-1$; in this example the solutions are $Ct+D/t$.

workedExamples.title: Test regularity
workedExamples.answer: A regular singular point; real positive-time solutions are sine and cosine of logarithmic time.

practice.problem: Is zero a regular singular point for $y''+y/t^3=0$?
practice.hint: Check time squared times the coefficient.
solution: $t^2Q=1/t$ is not analytic at zero.

practice.problem: Why must the leading Frobenius coefficient be nonzero?
practice.hint: Otherwise the stated starting power is not the lowest one.
solution: A zero leading term can be absorbed into a higher starting exponent.
practice.answer: It identifies the actual starting exponent.

practice.problem: Find the indicial roots of $t^2y''+2ty'=0$.
solution: The indicial equation is $r(r+1)$.

practice.problem: Can ordinary series and Frobenius be chosen without checking coefficients?
solution: Analyze the expansion point's singularity first.

commonMistakes.claim: Indicial roots are eigenvalues unrelated to starting powers.
commonMistakes.correction: They come from balancing the lowest powers.

commonMistakes.claim: Every solution stays finite at a regular singular point.
commonMistakes.correction: Negative powers or logarithms may diverge there.

lessons.concept: Near a regular singular point, a solution may need a power prefactor. Frobenius uses lowest-order balance to determine that exponent.
lessons.intuition: Ordinary Taylor series start at integer power zero; singularities may require a different initial scale.
objectives: Derive the indicial equation from lowest-order terms

formalDefinition.text: Regular singular points and indicial equations
conditions: $tP,t^2Q$ is analytic at zero. Construct solutions in the punctured neighborhood $t>0$, without claiming smooth passage through the singularity.

learningCheck.question: Which quantities are checked for a regular singular point?
learningCheck.explanation: These scaled coefficients measure singularity strength.

teaching.explain: Determine the singularity's strength before choosing a starting power rather than assuming an ordinary polynomial.

steps.title: Negative power
steps.observation: It grows near zero.
steps.instruction: Set starting power $r$ to $-1$ and positive time $t$ to $0.25$.

steps.title: Fractional power
steps.observation: The function tends to zero while its derivative may grow.
steps.instruction: Set starting power $r$ to $0.5$ and positive time $t$ to $0.25$.

steps.title: Integer power
steps.observation: Ordinary polynomials are special starting scales too.
steps.instruction: Set starting power $r$ to $2$ and positive time $t$ to $1$.

interactiveVisual.caption: Compare near-zero shapes for different starting powers. Changing this parameter also changes the equation. Only one solution is plotted, not a second-order general solution.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How do negative, fractional, and integer starting powers differ near zero?

lessons.title: Repeated indicial roots and logarithmic solutions
lessons.subtitle: One series is not every solution

body.title: Noninteger root differences
body.text: For the usual real-root regular-singular case, a noninteger difference allows two independent Frobenius constructions.

body.title: What about repeated roots?
body.text: Usually find one solution, then obtain the second by reduction of order. A logarithmic term may appear.

body.title: Integer difference does not force a logarithm
body.text: Some equations already have two pure-power solutions; others need logarithms. Inspect the recurrence or reduce order before asserting a form.

derivation.text: Take constant one as a known solution.
The reduction-of-order exponential factor is reciprocal time.
Integration gives an independent logarithmic solution.

workedExamples.title: Logarithmic independence
workedExamples.problem: Verify independence of $1,\ln t$ on positive time.
steps: It is nowhere zero on the positive interval.
workedExamples.answer: They form a complete fundamental pair.

workedExamples.title: Integer difference without a logarithm
workedExamples.problem: For $t^2y''-2y=0$, the roots differ by three. Is a logarithm required?
steps: The roots are two and minus one.

practice.problem: Does writing the same Frobenius solution twice work for a repeated root?
solution: Repetition supplies only one direction.

practice.problem: Does an integer root difference always give a nonzero logarithmic term?
solution: Distinct powers may already form the full solution.

practice.problem: Differentiate $\ln t$.
solution: Differentiate directly.

practice.problem: Does a logarithm diverging at zero contradict regular singularity?
practice.hint: Regularity constrains scaled coefficients, not finiteness of every solution.
solution: The definition permits this weak singularity.

commonMistakes.claim: A repeated indicial root supplies only one solution.
commonMistakes.correction: Second order still needs another independent solution.

commonMistakes.claim: Integer root differences automatically specify one logarithmic formula.
commonMistakes.correction: The actual recurrence or reduction determines the logarithmic term.

lessons.concept: Repeated or integer-separated roots may need a logarithmic second solution rather than two mechanically written power series.
lessons.intuition: When starting directions coincide, another form supplies the missing degree of freedom.
objectives: Recognize exceptions with integer root differences

body.title: An important equation
body.text: The order-zero Bessel equation is $t^2y''+ty'+t^2y=0$, with a regular singular point at zero.

body.title: How is its regular solution defined?
body.text: Choose the analytic solution finite at zero and normalized to one, called $J_0$. It is one solution; the second independent solution has a logarithmic singularity near zero.

body.title: Calculation and proof are separate
body.text: The recurrence supplies partial sums to any desired accuracy. A ratio test proves this series converges everywhere, while finite truncations remain approximate.

derivation.text: Substitute an ordinary power series into this special case.
Normalize the constant coefficient to one.

body.text: On a fixed finite interval with sufficient smoothness and state Lipschitz conditions, Euler has first-order global error as step size tends to zero. Do not cross singularities arbitrarily.

body.title: Explicit midpoint
body.text: Predict the midpoint with a half Euler step, then use its slope for the full step.

body.title: Heun's method
body.text: Predict the endpoint, then average slopes at the start and predicted endpoint. Unlike implicit trapezoidal stepping, it needs no equation solve.

body.title: What order means
body.text: With suitable smoothness, both have third-order one-step error and second-order global error. They generally differ on nonlinear problems.

derivation.text: Predict the endpoint with the current slope.

body.title: Our local-error convention
body.text: One-step local error compares an update from the exact starting state with the exact endpoint, without dividing by step size. Other books may normalize it, changing the stated power by one.

body.title: How do orders relate?
body.text: On a smooth finite interval with stable error propagation, an order-$p$ method usually has one-step error $O(h^{p+1})$ and global error $O(h^p)$.

body.title: How do you check a calculation?
body.text: Compare step sizes at the same endpoint. Theoretical error ratios suggest the asymptotic regime, but two close approximations may share bias and do not prove exactness.

derivation.text: Split endpoint error into new error and propagated error.
On a fixed interval, step count is inversely proportional to step size.
Stable accumulation leaves one less power in global error.

body.title: The test equation
body.text: For $y'=\lambda y$, an update has form $y_{n+1}=R(h\lambda)y_n$. Decay requires an amplification-factor magnitude below one.

body.title: Euler's restriction
body.text: Explicit Euler has $R(z)=1+z$. Its negative-real stability interval is $-2<h\lambda<0$. Boundary magnitudes equal one and do not reproduce decay.

body.title: What is stiffness?
body.text: Rapidly decaying modes can force explicit steps far smaller than slow-process accuracy requires. Implicit Euler's negative-real-axis stability removes this restriction, but accuracy still needs control.

derivation.text: Apply explicit Euler to the test equation.
On negative real roots, keep the factor strictly between minus one and one.
Implicit Euler evaluates the right side at the new state.

body.title: How is error estimated?
body.text: From the same start, compare one step $h$ with two steps $h/2$. For order $p$ in the asymptotic regime, fine-step local error is approximately their difference divided by $2^p-1$.

body.title: How is a step accepted?
body.text: Compare estimated error with combined absolute and relative tolerances. If too large, reduce the step and retry. Rejected states are not completed progress.

body.title: A complete workflow
body.text: Check domain, events, and known jumps, then choose method and tolerances. Record accepted steps and estimates, and verify through refinement or independent calculation. Report minimum-step or maximum-step stops rather than claiming success.

derivation.text: Let the coarse leading local error be $Ch^{p+1}$.
Two half steps reduce the leading error by factor $2^p$.
Divide the difference by the scale-ratio difference to estimate fine-step error.
